description:
Section 10(ii)(a), as quoted, addresses a landlord's eviction application where the Controller, after giving the tenant an opportunity to show cause, is satisfied that the tenant transferred lease rights or sublet all or part of the building without the landlord's written consent when the lease itself confers no such right.
The quoted provision supplies a statutory ground on which the Controller may direct eviction. Section 2(ix) defines tenant by reference to rent liability, includes specified surviving family members and persons remaining after termination, and excludes a person placed in occupation by the tenant.
This is quoted historical statutory text from the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, specifically ss. 10(ii)(a) and 2(ix). It does not establish Delhi law, a general rule for amalgamations, or current statutory applicability.
Judicially quoted statutory material preserved in a Supreme Court of India decision; the supplied unit does not certify the complete statute history or present applicability.

General Radio was the tenant under a 1959 rent agreement. A Bombay High Court order sanctioned its company-proposed amalgamation under Companies Act ss. 391 and 394, transferring and vesting its property, leases and tenancy rights in National Ekco; General Radio was dissolved. The passage records no written landlord consent and also refers to a lease clause prohibiting subletting without written permission.
The Court treated the amalgamation as a transfer of the tenant company's interest and rejected characterization of it as an involuntary transfer merely because a court sanctioned the scheme. It further stated that National Ekco could not be deemed a tenant under the Andhra Pradesh Act merely because tenancy rights vested in it under the amalgamation order.
The application is tied to this company-proposed ss. 391/394 amalgamation, the Andhra Pradesh rent statute, and the particular tenancy agreement. It does not state a general rule for every statutory acquisition or every rent-control regime.
Adopted judicial application by the Supreme Court of India within the historical statutory and factual setting supplied.

The unit reports Parasaram Harnand Rao v. Shanti Prasad Narinder Kumar Jain, involving tenancy rights of Laxmi Bank sold by an official liquidator during winding-up proceedings, confirmation of that sale by the High Court, subsequent possession by the purchaser, and later proceedings under the Delhi Rent Control Act.
As reported here, the Supreme Court in Parasaram held that the amplitude of Delhi Rent Control Act s. 14(b) covered a sublease, assignment, or other mode of parting with possession and was broad enough not to exclude an involuntary sale.
The reported proposition concerns Delhi rent law in the described liquidation-sale setting. This unit does not supply the complete Parasaram opinion and does not establish a separate holding about bank-acquisition statutes, company amalgamation, or other rent statutes.
Reported precedent described inside the General Radio judgment; it must not be treated as a newly adopted holding independently extracted from the full Parasaram opinion.

The Court relied on admissions and correspondence indicating that the flat had been given to Esso Standard Inc. on leave and licence in December 1968 and that the arrangement continued through renewals. It inferred a subsisting licence on 1 February 1973, before the later acquisition, and treated Esso Eastern Inc. as having acquired deemed-tenant or protected-licensee status under Bombay Rent Act s. 15A.
The Court held the contrary appellate findings erroneous and stated that the later acquisition did not extinguish the relevant status merely because a licence was personal, because the predecessor had already acquired statutory protection before the acquisition. The passage also refers to tenancy rights vesting in the Central Government under s. 5.
The reasoning concerns the particular licence history, the statutory date under s. 15A, and the later Esso acquisition. It does not establish a generic consequence for every licence, amalgamation, or acquisition.
Adopted Supreme Court reasoning in the supplied historical Bombay Rent Act and acquisition context.

The passage states that under s. 3 of the specific Acquisition Act, Esso Eastern Inc.'s rights, title and interest in its Indian undertakings transferred to and vested in the Central Government from the appointed day. Under s. 5(1) the Central Government became lessee or tenant, while s. 5(2) provided for renewal on the same terms if desired. It then describes a notification vesting those rights in Esso Standard Refining Company of India Ltd. and a later s. 396 amalgamation and name change to Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd.
On these stated statutory and corporate steps, the Court concluded that Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. was protected under s. 15A of the Bombay Rent Act. It found it unnecessary to decide the separate Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act s. 91 contention.
This is specific to the Esso Acquisition Act provisions, the identified notification, the 1974 s. 396 amalgamation, and Bombay Rent Act s. 15A. It does not create general immunity from rent-control or eviction provisions for statutory transfers or amalgamations.
Adopted Supreme Court treatment of the specified statutory vesting chain and resulting protection in this historical setting.

At the scheme-sanction stage, the Delhi High Court stated prima facie that contractual or statutory tenancy rights of a transferor company were transferable on amalgamation through the court's vesting order. It provisionally considered such vesting not to require landlord consent and outside the mischief of Delhi Rent Control Act s. 14(1)(b).
The Court expressly left undecided whether the post-amalgamation transfer could nevertheless amount to an assignment attracting eviction or other civil relief. It stated that no landlord cause of action accrued before amalgamation and vesting, that any such cause would arise afterward, and that the landlord remained free to pursue available proceedings before the appropriate authority.
The prima facie observation concerns company-scheme sanction and does not finally decide the Delhi rent-control eviction question. Any later assignment issue was reserved for the special rent jurisdiction or a maintainable civil action.
Judicial prima facie observation from a partial Delhi High Court document; the consequential eviction/assignment issue is expressly reserved and therefore is not a final holding on s. 14(1)(b).

A banking-company amalgamation under section 44A requires a draft scheme placed separately before each company's shareholders, approval by a majority in number representing two-thirds in value of shareholders present personally or by proxy, and submission of the approved scheme to the Reserve Bank for sanction.
If the Reserve Bank sanctions the scheme in writing, it binds the banking companies and shareholders; the amalgamated company's property and liabilities transfer to the acquiring banking company by virtue of the sanction order, subject to the sanctioned scheme. The Reserve Bank may separately direct dissolution.
This unit governs the section 44A procedure for amalgamation of banking companies, including meeting notice, dissenting-shareholder valuation rights, sanction, vesting, dissolution and evidentiary consequences. It does not itself establish immunity from lease, tenancy or rent restrictions. Central Government amalgamation power identified in subsection (7) is preserved, subject to consultation with the Reserve Bank.
Text of section 44A from an official Department of Financial Services consolidation identified as amended through 2021; the supplied metadata expressly leaves historical-version applicability unverified.

Where the Reserve Bank considers there is good reason, it may seek a Central Government moratorium for a banking company. During a moratorium or at any other time, the Reserve Bank may prepare a reconstruction or amalgamation scheme when satisfied that this is necessary in the public interest, depositors' interests, proper management, or the interests of the banking system as a whole.
After the draft consultation process, the Central Government may sanction the scheme with or without modifications. From the operative date, the sanctioned scheme binds specified companies, members, depositors, creditors, employees and other persons with relevant rights or liabilities; property, assets and liabilities transfer to the transferee bank only to the extent provided in the scheme.
Section 45 supplies the RBI/Central Government moratorium, reconstruction and amalgamation regime and permits scheme provisions concerning assets, liabilities, proceedings, creditor and member interests, employees and consequential matters. Section 45 and schemes under it override contrary laws, agreements, awards or instruments. Any modification or exemption concerning law governing acquired business is recommendation-based and limited to seven years. The text does not itself identify lease or rent-control consequences.
Text of section 45 from an official Department of Financial Services consolidation identified as amended through 2021; historical-version applicability remains unverified, and an individual sanctioned scheme remains necessary to determine its particular operative provisions.

Under section 9 of the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1980, the Central Government may, after consultation with the Reserve Bank, make a scheme to carry out the Act. The scheme-making power expressly extends to reconstitution, amalgamation, and transfer of all or part of specified banking undertakings.
For a scheme concerning the matters in section 9(2)(c), section 9(5) makes the scheme binding on the affected banks, corporations, members, depositors, creditors, employees and other persons having relevant rights or liabilities. Properties, assets and liabilities transfer and vest by virtue of, and only to the extent provided in, the scheme.
This unit concerns corresponding new banks and banking institutions under the 1980 Act and the statutory machinery for schemes. It does not itself specify the terms of any particular amalgamation, confer general immunity from lease or rent restrictions, or establish how a particular lease is treated. Parliament may modify or annul a laid scheme prospectively without prejudicing prior acts under it.
Statutory provision reproduced from an official Government of India consolidation. The supplied source status states that the consolidation cutoff is unknown and the historical version is unverified; the stored text also contains OCR artifacts.

The New Bank of India (Amalgamation and Transfer of Undertaking) Scheme, 1993 was made under section 9 of the 1980 Act after consultation with the Reserve Bank. A contemporaneous notification appointed 4 September 1993 as its commencement date. The Scheme identifies New Bank of India as transferor and Punjab National Bank as transferee.
On commencement, New Bank of India's undertakings transfer to and vest in Punjab National Bank, including specified assets, rights, obligations and liabilities. Property held under lease is treated as leased to the transferee as if the lease had been granted to it, with lease rights transferred and vested. Existing instruments and proceedings generally continue with the transferee substituted for the transferor.
The Scheme is specific to the New Bank of India-to-Punjab National Bank amalgamation and does not automatically govern other bank mergers. It separately addresses foreign assets where local law prevents the Scheme alone from effecting transfer. Although it expressly transfers leasehold status and rights, the supplied text does not state a general exemption from landlord-consent requirements, rent-control legislation, eviction law or other lease restrictions.
Original 1993 Gazette scheme and commencement notification as preserved by the Government of India source. It is an operative event-specific scheme issued under section 9, subject to the supplied OCR text and without independent certification here of the complete surrounding statutory history.
